blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher who wants experienced-level depth, in the style of the Java Full Stack guides. Every example titled `*.py` was run when this page was built, on Python 3.12.13 with FastAPI 0.162.0, Pydantic 2.14.2, SQLAlchemy 2.1.8, Django 6.1.3, and the output shown is what it really printed. Python and its libraries change quickly (and some examples need servers that a build cannot start, so those are only syntax-checked): check the official documentation for anything newer before relying on a detail.

Core Python is fifteen Parts. Read straight through without a plan and most people stall in the collections chapters and never reach concurrency or CPython internals, which are exactly the topics that separate a fresher from an experienced developer. This plan fits the whole of Core Python into **25 study days** over four weeks, about **2 to 3 hours a day**, with one rest day each week.

| Block | Time | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Read** | 40% | The day's chapters, with a REPL open. Type every example |
| **Run and break** | 30% | Change the examples, predict the output, run, explain the difference |
| **Retrieve** | 30% | Without the page: the chapter's practice questions, the "what does this print" puzzles, then 2 coding problems |

#### The error log

Keep a plain text file called `errors.txt`. For every question you get wrong, write one line: the topic, what you answered, and the correct idea **in your own words**. At the end of each week re-read only that file. Your own mistakes are the most efficient syllabus there is.

### Week 1: the language, objects and design (days 1 to 7)

Goal: you can explain names versus objects, write idiomatic functions and classes, and say what `==`, `is`, mutability and the MRO mean without notes.

| Day | Read | Code focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Part 1: platform, bytecode, object model, toolchain | Create a venv or `uv` project; inspect bytecode with `dis`; the Java crosswalk table |
| 2 | Part 2: names, types, operators, conversions | Floats, `Decimal`, truthiness puzzles; chained comparisons |
| 3 | Part 2: control flow, slicing, unpacking, functions, I/O | `match`; mutable default trap; closures; `argparse` mini-tool |
| 4 | Part 3: classes, properties, inheritance and the MRO | Bank-style class with `@property`; draw an MRO diamond and verify with `__mro__` |
| 5 | Part 3: dunder methods, ABC and Protocol, dataclasses, enums | A `Vector` and a `Money` value object with full comparison and hashing |
| 6 | Re-read the error log; Part 3 practice questions; puzzles 1 to 15 | Predict first, then run each puzzle |
| 7 | Rest, or one DSA problem | |

### Week 2: text, errors, files, collections and iterators (days 8 to 13)

Goal: you handle text and time correctly, write robust file and error handling, and choose the right container with its Big-O.

| Day | Read | Code focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | Part 4: strings, regex, Unicode, numbers, dates | A log-line parser with named groups; UTC datetimes with `zoneinfo` |
| 9 | Part 5: exceptions, context managers, logging | A custom exception hierarchy; a `@contextmanager` timer; `logging` configuration |
| 10 | Part 5: files, `pathlib`, serialization, OS interface | Atomic file write; JSON round trip; a safe `subprocess` call |
| 11 | Part 6: lists, dicts, sets, sorting, heaps, deques | `Counter`, `defaultdict`, `heapq` top-k; multi-key sorting |
| 12 | Part 6: implement your own array list, hash map, LRU cache | Write each from memory, then diff with the page |
| 13 | Part 7: comprehensions, iterators, generators, `itertools`, decorators intro | A generator pipeline over a big file; `@retry` decorator |

### Week 3: concurrency, CPython and runtime features (days 14 to 19)

Goal: you can choose between threads, processes and asyncio, explain the GIL and reference counting, and read what a framework does with decorators, descriptors and signatures.

| Day | Read | Code focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 | Part 8: concurrency concepts, the GIL, threads, locks | The race and deadlock demos; fix them |
| 15 | Part 8: thread pools, futures, processes | `ThreadPoolExecutor` vs `ProcessPoolExecutor` timing on your own machine |
| 16 | Part 9: event loop, tasks, `TaskGroup`, timeouts, semaphores | Async fetcher with a concurrency limit |
| 17 | Part 9: blocking code in async, streams, pitfalls | Reproduce the "blocked loop" bug and fix it with `to_thread` |
| 18 | Part 10: object model, reference counting, GC, leaks, bytecode | A `tracemalloc` leak hunt; `cProfile` a slow function |
| 19 | Part 11: decorators, descriptors, metaclasses, imports, diagnostics | A validated descriptor; an `__init_subclass__` registry; `faulthandler` |

### Week 4: tooling, practice and interviews (days 20 to 25)

Goal: you write tested, typed, linted, packaged code, and you can solve and explain interview problems under time.

| Day | Read | Code focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | Part 12: types, modern Python, pytest | Add hints and run `mypy --strict`; write fixtures and `parametrize` |
| 21 | Part 12: packaging, ruff, pre-commit; Part 13 patterns | `pyproject.toml`; the refactor exercise; strategy and observer |
| 22 | Part 13: secure coding; Part 14 Projects A and B | SQL injection and password-hash demos; build the bank and the log analyzer |
| 23 | Part 14 Projects C and D | Concurrent processor and key-value store with tests |
| 24 | Part 15: Q&A banks, puzzles 16 to 31, coding problems | Timed: 3 problems in 60 minutes, spoken aloud |
| 25 | The part-by-part quizzes, then the final mock interview | Score it; write the error log; plan the next stage (DSA and FastAPI) |

Two DSA problems a day (the DSA stage next in this tree), one small project per month that you deploy, and one new standard-library module per week (`itertools`, `functools`, `contextlib`, `pathlib`, `statistics`...). Fluency comes from range, not from re-reading.
blocks.title: After day 25 keep three habits

blocks.text:
These tables are meant to be scanned, not read. They compress the tree into reference pages you can review the night before an interview or keep open while coding. Each says where the full explanation lives.

### Keywords, built-in types and truth values (Parts 1 and 2)

| Group | Keywords (Python 3.12: 35) |
| --- | --- |
| Values | `True`, `False`, `None` |
| Logic | `and`, `or`, `not`, `is`, `in` |
| Flow | `if`, `elif`, `else`, `for`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, `pass`, `match`\*, `case`\* |
| Functions and classes | `def`, `return`, `lambda`, `yield`, `class`, `global`, `nonlocal`, `del` |
| Errors and resources | `try`, `except`, `finally`, `raise`, `assert`, `with`, `as` |
| Modules | `import`, `from` |
| Async | `async`, `await` |

\* soft keywords, usable as names elsewhere (also `type` and `_`).

| Type | Mutable | Hashable | Ordered | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int`, `float`, `bool`, `complex` | no | yes | n/a | numbers (`int` unbounded; money uses `Decimal`) |
| `str` | no | yes | yes | text (Unicode) |
| `bytes` / `bytearray` | no / yes | yes / no | yes | binary data |
| `tuple` | no | if items are | yes | records, dict keys |
| `list` | yes | no | yes | growable sequence |
| `dict` | yes | no | insertion order | key to value |
| `set` / `frozenset` | yes / no | no / yes | no | uniqueness, membership |
| `None` | no | yes | n/a | no value |

Falsy: `None`, `False`, any numeric zero, and empty `""`, `b""`, `[]`, `()`, `{}`, `set()`, `range(0)`. Everything else is truthy (including `"0"` and `[0]`).

### Operators and precedence (Part 2)

| Tightest to loosest | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `(...)`, `[...]`, `{...}`, `x.attr`, `x[i]`, `f(...)` |
| 2 | `**` (right-associative; `-2 ** 2 == -4`) |
| 3 | unary `+x`, `-x`, `~x` |
| 4 | `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `@` |
| 5 | `+`, `-` |
| 6 | `<<`, `>>` |
| 7 | `&`, then `^`, then `\|` |
| 8 | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `!=`, `==`, `in`, `not in`, `is`, `is not` (chain: `a < b < c`) |
| 9 | `not x`, then `and`, then `or` |
| 10 | `x if cond else y`, `lambda`, `:=` |

`/` always returns `float`; `//` floors toward minus infinity; `%` takes the sign of the divisor; `round()` is banker's rounding; `and`/`or` return an operand and short-circuit.

### Strings, formatting and text (Part 4)

| Task | Code |
| --- | --- |
| Trim, split, join | `s.strip()`, `s.split(",")`, `s.partition("=")`, `",".join(parts)` |
| Test | `s.startswith(("a", "b"))`, `s.isdigit()`, `"x" in s`, `s.casefold()` |
| Replace | `s.replace(a, b)`, `s.translate(table)`, `re.sub(p, r, s)` |
| f-string spec | `f"{x:>10.2f}"` align, width, precision; `{x:,}` thousands; `{x:08b}` binary; `{x!r}`; `{x=}`; `{d:%Y-%m-%d}` |
| Regex | `re.search`, `match` (start), `fullmatch` (validate), `findall`, `finditer`, `sub`, named groups `(?P<n>...)`, raw strings |
| Bytes | `s.encode("utf-8")`, `b.decode("utf-8")`; always name the encoding; `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)` |
| Money and decimals | `Decimal("0.10")`, `quantize`; integers of the smallest unit |
| Time | UTC and aware: `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`; `astimezone(ZoneInfo(...))`; `isoformat` / `fromisoformat` |

### Containers and their costs (Part 6)

| Structure | Add | Lookup | Remove | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list` | `append` O(1) am. | `x in l` O(n), `l[i]` O(1) | `pop()` O(1), `pop(0)`/`remove` O(n) | `sort` O(n log n), stable |
| `dict` | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | insertion-ordered; hashable keys |
| `set` | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | `\| & - ^`; no order |
| `deque` | both ends O(1) | O(n) middle | both ends O(1) | queue, sliding window |
| `heapq` | `heappush` O(log n) | min at `h[0]` O(1) | `heappop` O(log n) | min-heap; negate for max |
| `bisect` | `insort` O(n) | `bisect_left` O(log n) | n/a | sorted list |
| `Counter`, `defaultdict`, `OrderedDict`, `ChainMap` | | | | counting, grouping, recency, layering |

### Methods worth knowing cold

| Object | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | `append`, `extend`, `insert`, `pop`, `remove`, `index`, `count`, `sort`, `reverse`, `copy`, `clear` |
| `dict` | `get`, `setdefault`, `pop`, `popitem`, `update`, `items`, `keys`, `values`, `fromkeys`, `\|` (3.9+) |
| `set` | `add`, `discard`, `remove`, `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `issubset`, `isdisjoint` |
| builtins | `len`, `sum`, `min`, `max` (`key=`, `default=`), `sorted`, `reversed`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `map`, `filter`, `any`, `all`, `range`, `isinstance`, `getattr`, `iter`, `next` |

### Comprehensions, unpacking and generators (Part 7)

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `[f(x) for x in xs if p(x)]` | list comprehension |
| `{k: v for k, v in pairs}`, `{x for x in xs}` | dict and set comprehensions |
| `(f(x) for x in xs)` | generator expression (lazy, one pass) |
| `a, *rest = items`; `first, *_, last = items` | star unpacking |
| `f(*args, **kwargs)`; `{**a, **b}`; `[*a, *b]` | spread into calls and literals |
| `yield`, `yield from` | generator; delegate |
| `itertools`: `chain`, `islice`, `product`, `permutations`, `combinations`, `accumulate`, `groupby` (sorted!), `pairwise`, `batched` | iterator toolbox |
| `functools`: `partial`, `reduce`, `cache`, `lru_cache`, `singledispatch`, `cached_property`, `wraps` | function tools |

### Classes and the data model (Part 3)

| Need | Write |
| --- | --- |
| Readable debug output | `__repr__` (always), `__str__` |
| Equality and hashing | `__eq__` plus `__hash__` (immutable fields only) |
| Ordering | `__lt__` + `@total_ordering`, or `@dataclass(order=True)` |
| Container behaviour | `__len__`, `__getitem__`, `__iter__`, `__contains__` |
| Callable object | `__call__` |
| Context manager | `__enter__`, `__exit__` or `@contextmanager` |
| Arithmetic | `__add__`, `__radd__`, `__mul__`, `__neg__`, return `NotImplemented` for unknown types |
| Attribute control | `@property`, descriptors (`__get__`, `__set__`), `__getattr__`, `__slots__` |
| Data holder | `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)`, `NamedTuple`, `Enum`, `TypedDict` |
| Contract | `abc.ABC` + `@abstractmethod`, `typing.Protocol` |

### Exceptions, files and the OS (Part 5)

| Task | Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Handle | `try: ... except (A, B) as e: ... else: ... finally: ...` |
| Wrap with cause | `raise DomainError("...") from e` |
| Common built-ins | `ValueError` bad value; `TypeError` wrong type; `KeyError`/`IndexError`; `AttributeError`; `FileNotFoundError`; `ZeroDivisionError`; `StopIteration`; `RecursionError` |
| Read a file | `with open(p, encoding="utf-8") as f: for line in f:` |
| Paths | `Path(...) / "x"`, `.read_text()`, `.write_text()`, `.glob()`, `.exists()`, `.resolve().is_relative_to(base)` |
| Modes | `r` read, `w` truncate, `a` append, `x` exclusive create, `b` binary |
| JSON | `json.dumps(obj, indent=2)`, `json.loads(s)`; `default=` for unsupported types |
| Subprocess | `subprocess.run([...], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=...)` |
| Logging | `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`; `log.info("x %s", v)`; `log.exception("...")` |

### Concurrency and asyncio (Parts 8 and 9)

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| I/O-bound, few blocking calls | `ThreadPoolExecutor` |
| I/O-bound, very many connections | `asyncio` with async libraries |
| CPU-bound | `ProcessPoolExecutor` (needs `if __name__ == "__main__":`), or native libraries |
| Shared mutable state | `Lock`; or `queue.Queue`; or avoid sharing |
| Deadlock | Same global lock order; timeouts; short critical sections |
| GIL | One thread runs bytecode at a time; 3.13 and 3.14 offer a free-threaded build |

| asyncio | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `asyncio.run(main())` | single entry point |
| `await asyncio.gather(*aws)` / `TaskGroup` | run together (prefer `TaskGroup`) |
| `async with asyncio.timeout(s)` | deadline |
| `asyncio.Semaphore(n)`, `asyncio.Queue` | concurrency limit, worker pool |
| `await asyncio.to_thread(fn)` | blocking call off the loop |
| `task.cancel()` and `except CancelledError: raise` | cancellation |
| Never | `time.sleep`, `requests`, heavy CPU inside `async def` |

### CPython, performance and memory (Part 10)

| Topic | Fact |
| --- | --- |
| Memory | Reference counting plus a generational cycle collector; pymalloc arenas |
| Leaks | Unbounded caches, globals, registries; find with `tracemalloc` snapshot diffs |
| Speed | Fix the algorithm; built-ins and NumPy; `lru_cache`; `timeit` / `cProfile` / `py-spy` |
| Bytecode | `dis.dis(f)`; 3.11+ specialises hot instructions |
| Objects | Header (refcount, type) + data; `sys.getsizeof` is shallow; `__slots__` saves memory |

### Types, tests and packaging (Part 12)

| Task | Tool or syntax |
| --- | --- |
| Hints | `list[int]`, `dict[str, int]`, `int \| None`, `Callable[[int], str]`, `Literal["a"]`, `TypedDict`, `Protocol`, `def f[T](x: T) -> T` (3.12) |
| Check types | `mypy --strict` or `pyright` |
| Test | `pytest -q -x -k expr --cov`; fixtures, `parametrize`, `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch`, `pytest.raises` |
| Quality | `ruff check . --fix`, `ruff format .`, `pre-commit` |
| Project | `pyproject.toml`; `uv init`, `uv add`, `uv sync`, `uv run`, `uv build` |
| Version | `requires-python = ">=3.12"`; pin and lock applications; range libraries |

### Security checklist (Part 13)

Parameterised SQL; `subprocess` with a list and no `shell=True`; no `eval` or `pickle` on untrusted data; `secrets` for tokens; Argon2 or bcrypt for passwords; validate paths and outbound URLs; `verify=True` for TLS; secrets from the environment; generic error messages to clients.

sections.title: Final Mock Interview and What to Do Next

blocks.text:
The last section of this part is a **single mixed test** (the "Final Mock Interview" below the cheat sheets, after the part quizzes). Treat it like the real thing: set a timer for **60 minutes**, close the page, and answer on paper before you reveal anything. The questions are a blend of recall and "what does this print" items, and every snippet was run when this page was built.

How to read your score:

| Score | Meaning | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 27 to 30 of 30 | Interview-ready on core Python | Move on to the DSA and FastAPI stages; keep the error log |
| 22 to 26 | Solid, with specific gaps | Re-read the Parts behind each miss, redo the puzzles |
| 16 to 21 | Fundamentals shaky | Repeat weeks 1 and 2 of the plan before moving on |
| Below 16 | Not yet | Go back to Parts 2 and 3 and rebuild the foundations; build Projects A and B |

Structure the answer in five beats: **the problem** in one sentence, **the design** (two or three modules or classes and why), **one hard bug** you found and how (the debugging method from Part 11), **what you would change** at ten times the load, and **how you tested it**. Prepare this for Projects A to D of Part 14, and for the Library API in the FastAPI stage. Specifics beat adjectives: "I used a `deque` for O(1) pops" beats "I optimised it".
blocks.title: "Tell me about a Python project you built."

blocks.text: For every miss, write a three-line program that demonstrates the correct behaviour and run it. Predicting, running and seeing the real output is what converts a wrong belief into a correct one.
blocks.title: After the mock, do not just read the key
Key points
blocks.text:
- Plan: 25 days, three blocks a day, an error log
- Cheat sheets are for review, not first reading
- Quizzes and the mock test recall under time pressure
- Score below 22 means repeat the weaker weeks
- Move on to DSA and FastAPI with two problems a day

A single mixed test of everything in Core Python. Set a timer for 60 minutes, close the page and answer on paper first. 27 or more correct means interview-ready on the language; below 16 means repeat weeks 1 and 2 of the plan. Every program was run when this page was built. 30 original questions on 29 areas; pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a[:]
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)
```
items.w: A full slice makes a shallow copy: a new list, so changing `b[0]` does not affect `a`.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print([i for i in range(10) if i % 2][-1], 7 // 2 * 2 + 7 % 2)
```
items.w: The odd numbers below 10 end with 9. `7 // 2 * 2` is 6 (left to right), plus `7 % 2` which is 1, gives 7.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
d = {"a": 1}
d2 = d
d2["b"] = 2
print(len(d), d is d2)
```
items.w: `d2 = d` makes a second name for the same dictionary.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
s = "hello"
print(s[1:4], s[::-1][:2], s.find("z"))
```
items.w: `s[1:4]` is `ell`; reversing gives `olleh` whose first two characters are `ol`; `find` returns `-1` when absent.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
try:
    int("x")
except ValueError:
    print("a")
else:
    print("b")
finally:
    print("c")
```
items.w: The error is handled (`a`), `else` is skipped because an exception occurred, and `finally` always runs (`c`).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
def gen():
    yield 1
    return 2
g = gen()
print(next(g))
try:
    next(g)
except StopIteration as stop:
    print(stop.value)
```
items.w: A generator's `return` value travels in `StopIteration.value`; `yield from` uses it.
Each `inc` returns `self`, so calls chain (a fluent interface).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(sorted(["b", "A", "c"], key=str.lower), max("apple", "Apple"))
```
items.w: Sorting with `key=str.lower` compares `a, b, c`, giving `A, b, c`. `max` compares by code point and lowercase `a` (97) is greater than `A` (65).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import copy
x = {"k": [1]}
y = copy.deepcopy(x)
y["k"].append(2)
print(x)
```
items.w: `deepcopy` duplicates the nested list, so appending to the copy leaves the original unchanged.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(bool([]), bool([[]]), bool(0.0), bool("0"))
```
items.w: An empty list is falsy; a list holding an empty list has one element, so it is truthy; `0.0` is falsy; the string `"0"` is non-empty, so truthy.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(type(1 / 2).__name__, type(1 // 2).__name__, 2 ** -1)
```
items.w: `/` always returns a float, `//` of two ints returns an int, and a negative exponent gives a float.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
d["a"] += 1
print(d["b"], dict(d))
```
items.w: Reading a missing key on a `defaultdict` inserts it with the default value, so `b` appears in the dictionary too.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
x = 5
def f():
    x = 10
    def g():
        nonlocal x
        x += 1
        return x
    return g()
print(f(), x)
```
items.w: `nonlocal` rebinds `f`'s local `x` (10 becomes 11); the global `x` is a different variable and stays 5.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
t = (1, [2, 3])
t[1].append(4)
print(t)
```
items.w: The tuple is immutable but holds a reference to a mutable list; the list can still change.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print({1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}, {1, 2} ^ {2, 3}, len({1, 1.0, "1"}))
```
items.w: Intersection is `{2, 3}`, symmetric difference `{1, 3}`, and `1` and `1.0` are the same set element, leaving two distinct elements.

items.q: *(Concept)* The time complexity of `my_list.insert(0, x)` for a list with n items is
items.w: Every existing element must shift one place to the right. A `deque` offers O(1) `appendleft`.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which approach gives a real speed-up for CPU-bound pure-Python work in the default (GIL) CPython build?
items.w: Processes each have their own interpreter and GIL. Threads and coroutines take turns on one core for pure-Python CPU work.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which statement about `is` is correct?
o: `x is y` is the same as `id(x) == id(y) + 1`
`is` compares object identity; use it for `None` and singletons, not for numbers or strings
items.w: Identity of equal numbers and strings is an implementation detail (caching, interning), so comparisons with `is` give unreliable results.

items.q: *(Concept)* `python -m venv .venv` creates
o: a copy of the operating system
an isolated directory with its own interpreter link and `site-packages` for one project
items.w: Virtual environments isolate dependencies per project; activate it or run its `python` directly.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why wrap async HTTP calls in `async with asyncio.Semaphore(10):` (or use a semaphore object)?
o: To limit how many run concurrently so the server (or your connection pool) is not overwhelmed
items.w: `gather` over thousands of items would open thousands of connections at once; a semaphore caps concurrency.

items.q: *(Concept)* Arguments of a function decorated with `@functools.lru_cache` must be
items.w: The cache is a dictionary keyed by the arguments, so lists and dicts raise `TypeError: unhashable type`.

items.q: *(Concept)* What is `__slots__` mainly for?
o: Fixing the set of instance attributes and removing the per-instance `__dict__`, saving memory for many small objects
items.w: Slots store attributes in fixed storage; the price is no dynamic attributes and some restrictions with multiple inheritance.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why can threads still speed up a program that downloads many files?
o: The operating system merges the downloads
The GIL does not exist for network code
The GIL is released while a thread waits on blocking I/O, so waits overlap
items.w: Waiting is not bytecode execution. That is why threads and asyncio work well for I/O-bound programs.

items.q: *(Concept)* What does the language guarantee about dictionary ordering since Python 3.7?
o: Order is random but stable per run
items.w: Insertion order is part of the language specification (it was a CPython detail in 3.6).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        t1 = tg.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0, "x"))
        t2 = tg.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0, "y"))
    print(t1.result() + t2.result())
asyncio.run(main())
```
items.w: The `async with` block waits for all tasks; `asyncio.sleep(0, "x")` returns `"x"`, and the strings are concatenated.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from functools import partial
add = lambda a, b, c: a + b + c
print(partial(add, 1, c=3)(2))
```
items.w: `partial(add, 1, c=3)` fixes `a=1` and `c=3`; calling it with `2` supplies `b`, so the result is 1 + 2 + 3.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(f"{3.14159:.2f} {42:05d} {255:x} {'a':*>3}|")
```
items.w: `.2f` is two decimals, `05d` zero-pads to width 5, `x` is lowercase hexadecimal, and `*>3` right-aligns in width 3 filling with `*`.

items.q: *(Concept)* What happens if your service calls `pickle.loads` on bytes a user sent?
o: The user can make your process run arbitrary code
items.w: Unpickling can call any importable function. Use JSON plus validation for untrusted data.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import re
print(re.findall(r"\b\w{3}\b", "the quick fox ran"))
```
items.w: `\b\w{3}\b` matches whole words of exactly three characters: `the`, `fox` and `ran`.

items.q: *(Concept)* An `async def` endpoint slows down as traffic rises, yet CPU use stays low. The most likely cause is
o: a blocking call (synchronous I/O or `time.sleep`) on the event loop, stalling every other request
items.w: A blocked loop cannot serve other tasks. Use async libraries, `asyncio.to_thread`, or declare the endpoint with `def` so the framework runs it in a thread pool.

blocks.text: Six questions per Part (1 to 14), mixing concepts and short programs. Answer closed-book, then check: the effort of recalling is what makes it stick. Every "what does this print" answer was produced by running the program. 84 original questions on 14 areas; pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q: *(Concept)* The reference implementation of Python, CPython, runs your source by
o: compiling it to bytecode (cached in .pyc files for imported modules) and interpreting that bytecode on a virtual machine
compiling it straight to machine code with a JIT
translating it to Java bytecode for the JVM
interpreting the source text line by line with no intermediate form
items.w: CPython tokenises, parses to an AST, compiles to a code object holding bytecode and runs it on its evaluation loop. Experimental JITs exist from 3.13, but the model is still bytecode plus interpreter.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which statement about `__pycache__` and `.pyc` files is correct?
o: They contain a copy of the source for faster reading
They hold machine code and can be shared between operating systems
They cache compiled bytecode of imported modules, and the file name carries the interpreter version, so several versions can coexist
They are required for the top-level script you run to start
items.w: Bytecode is specific to a Python version, which is why the name looks like `module.cpython-312.pyc`. The top-level script is compiled each time it runs. Do not commit them.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
a = int("300")
b = int("300")
print(a == b, a is b)
```
items.w: The values are equal, but each `int("300")` creates a separate object (only -5 to 256 are cached in CPython). Use `==` for values; `is` for `None` and singletons.

items.q: *(Concept)* What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` achieve?
o: It runs the block on every import
It runs the block only when the file is executed as a script, not when it is imported
It is required for functions to be defined
items.w: When a file is run directly, its `__name__` is `"__main__"`; when imported, it is the module's name. The guard keeps imports free of side effects.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
x = [1, 2]
y = x
y.append(3)
print(len(x), x is y)
```
items.w: `y = x` binds a second name to the same list; no copy is made, so the append is visible through `x`.

items.q: *(Concept)* `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'` appears right after you ran `pip install requests`. What should you check first?
o: Whether pip installed into the same interpreter that runs the script (`sys.executable`, and use `python -m pip`)
items.w: The classic cause is two Pythons: pip belongs to one, the script runs with another. `python -m pip` binds installation to the interpreter you name.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(-7 // 2, -7 % 2)
```
items.w: `//` floors toward minus infinity and `%` takes the sign of the divisor, so `(-7 // 2) * 2 + (-7 % 2) == -7`.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, round(2.5))
```
items.w: Binary floats cannot hold 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the sum is `0.30000000000000004`. `round` uses banker's rounding: ties go to the even neighbour, so 2.5 becomes 2.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which group contains only falsy values?
items.w: Falsy: `None`, `False`, numeric zero, and empty containers. `[0]` (a non-empty list) and the strings `"0"` and `"False"` are truthy.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
def add(x, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(x)
    return bucket
add(1)
print(add(2))
```
items.w: The default list is created once when `def` runs and shared by every call that omits it. Use `None` as the default and create the list inside.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print("a" "b" * 2, [1] * 2 + [2])
```
items.w: Adjacent string literals are joined at compile time, so `"a" "b"` is the single literal `"ab"` and then `* 2` repeats it. For the list, `*` binds tighter than `+`.

items.q: *(Concept)* Given `def f(a, /, b, *, c): ...`, which call is valid?
items.w: `a` is positional-only (before `/`), `b` may be positional or keyword, and `c` is keyword-only (after `*`). A positional argument cannot follow a keyword argument.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
class A:
    items = []
a, b = A(), A()
a.items.append(1)
print(b.items)
```
items.w: `items` is a class attribute: one list shared by all instances. Per-instance state belongs in `__init__`.

items.q: *(Concept)* In a class with several bases, `super()` refers to
o: the next class after the current one in the method resolution order of the instance's type
items.w: `super()` follows `type(self).__mro__`, which is what makes cooperative multiple inheritance (each method calling `super()`) run every class exactly once.
Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to `None`, so instances cannot be put in a set or used as dict keys.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which statement about `@dataclass` is true?
o: It checks the annotated types at run time and raises on a mismatch
It requires the class to inherit from a base class
It generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the annotated fields
items.w: Dataclasses remove boilerplate; they do not validate (use Pydantic for that). Options include `frozen`, `order`, `slots` and `kw_only`.
A property without a setter is read-only: assignment raises `AttributeError`.

items.q: *(Concept)* A binary operator method such as `__add__` should `return NotImplemented` when
o: it does not know how to handle the other operand's type, so Python can try the reflected method
items.w: Returning `NotImplemented` (not raising `NotImplementedError`) lets Python try `other.__radd__(self)` and finally raise `TypeError`.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(len("é"), len("é".encode()))
```
items.w: In the source file the character is one code point (`len` counts code points) and takes two bytes in UTF-8.

items.q: *(Concept)* The most reliable way to compare two user-entered strings ignoring case across languages is
items.w: `casefold` is built for caseless matching (it maps `ß` to `ss`, which `lower` does not).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import re
print(re.match(r"\d+", "abc123"), bool(re.search(r"\d+", "abc123")))
```
items.w: `match` only tries at the start of the string, where there is no digit; `search` finds the digits anywhere.

items.q: *(Concept)* The recommended practice for storing and computing timestamps is
o: strings in each user's local format
timezone-aware UTC values, converted to a local zone only for display
items.w: Aware UTC datetimes denote one instant, compare and subtract correctly, and survive daylight-saving changes. `utcnow()` returns a naive value and is deprecated since 3.12.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"), 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
```
items.w: `Decimal` built from strings does exact decimal arithmetic; binary floats do not.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why should you write `open(path, encoding="utf-8")`?
o: UTF-8 is required for text files to open at all
Without it Python uses the platform's default encoding, so the same code behaves differently on different machines
items.w: The default encoding depends on the locale (for example cp1252 on many Windows setups). Being explicit makes behaviour portable.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
def f():
    try:
        return "a"
    finally:
        print("b")
print(f())
```
items.w: `finally` runs before the function actually returns, so `b` is printed first, then the returned `a`.

items.q: *(Concept)* A bare `except:` differs from `except Exception:` in that it also catches
o: `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, so Ctrl-C and `sys.exit()` stop working
items.w: `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` derive from `BaseException`, not `Exception`. Catching them by accident makes programs hard to stop.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
try:
    {}["k"]
except (KeyError, IndexError) as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
```
items.w: Looking up a missing key raises `KeyError` (a subclass of `LookupError`); the tuple lets one handler cover several types.

items.q: *(Concept)* `with open(path) as f:` guarantees that
o: the file is locked against other processes
the file is closed when the block exits, even if an exception is raised
items.w: `with` calls `__exit__` however the block ends, which is deterministic cleanup.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import json
print(json.loads(json.dumps({"a": (1, 2)})))
```
items.w: JSON has no tuples, so a tuple comes back as a list. Note that Python prints dicts with single quotes.

items.q: *(Concept)* Loading a pickle file that a user uploaded is dangerous because
o: unpickling can call arbitrary functions, so it can execute attacker-chosen code
the pickle format changes every release
items.w: `pickle.loads` rebuilds objects by calling callables named in the data. Use JSON or another data-only format for untrusted input.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(nums.sort(), sorted(nums))
```
items.w: `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`; `sorted` returns a new list.

items.q: *(Concept)* You must test membership of millions of values against the same collection of 100,000 ids. The best structure for the ids is
items.w: A set hashes the value (O(1) on average) while list and tuple scan linearly (O(n)).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
d = {}
d.setdefault("a", []).append(1)
d.setdefault("a", []).append(2)
print(d)
```
items.w: `setdefault` returns the existing list when the key is present, so both appends go to the same list.

items.q: *(Concept)* For a FIFO queue with frequent removal from the front, the right container is
items.w: `list.pop(0)` is O(n) because every element shifts; `deque.popleft()` is O(1).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))
```
items.w: `banana` has three `a`, two `n` and one `b`; `most_common(1)` returns a list holding the top (item, count) pair.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which of these cannot be used as a dictionary key?
items.w: Keys must be hashable. Lists are mutable and unhashable; tuples of hashables, strings and frozensets are fine.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
g = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
print(list(g), list(g))
```
items.w: A generator is a one-shot iterator: the first `list` exhausts it.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fs])
```
items.w: Closures capture the variable `i`, not its value; after the loop it is 2. Bind the value with a default argument (`lambda i=i: i`).

items.q: *(Concept)* `yield from other()` inside a generator
o: returns all values as one list
delegates to the other generator, forwards its values and evaluates to its return value
items.w: It is generator delegation: values (and sent values and exceptions) pass through, and the sub-generator's `return` value becomes the result of the expression.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from itertools import accumulate, count, islice
print(list(islice(accumulate(count(1)), 5)))
```
items.w: `accumulate` gives running totals of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ...; `islice` takes the first five from the infinite stream.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why do decorators use `functools.wraps`?
o: It is required, or the code raises a SyntaxError
To make the decorated function immutable
To make the wrapper run faster
To copy the wrapped function's name, docstring and signature metadata onto the wrapper
items.w: Without it the decorated function reports the wrapper's name and loses its documentation and signature, which breaks debugging and frameworks that read signatures.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
print(sum(x for x in range(10) if x % 3 == 0), list(map(str.upper, "ab")))
```
items.w: The multiples of 3 below 10 are 0, 3, 6 and 9 (sum 18); `map` applies `str.upper` to each character.

items.q: *(Concept)* In standard CPython, what does the GIL prevent?
o: Two threads from executing Python bytecode at the same instant in one interpreter
items.w: CPU-bound pure-Python threads take turns. Blocking I/O releases the GIL, and separate processes have separate GILs.

items.q: *(Concept)* You must make 200 independent HTTP calls with the blocking `requests` library. The most suitable simple tool is
o: `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded number of workers
items.w: The work is I/O-bound: threads overlap the waiting, because the GIL is released during network I/O. Bound the pool to be polite to the server.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
with ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as pool:
    print(list(pool.map(lambda n: n * n, range(4))))
```
o: it depends on the thread scheduling
items.w: `Executor.map` returns results in the order of the inputs, regardless of which task finishes first.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why is `if __name__ == "__main__":` mandatory around multiprocessing code on Windows and macOS?
o: Because `fork` is not available in Python
Child processes are started with `spawn`, which re-imports the main module; without the guard the import would start processes recursively
items.w: `spawn` starts a fresh interpreter and imports the module to find the target function; the guard stops that import from running the process-starting code again.

items.q: *(Concept)* The standard way to rule out a deadlock between two locks is to
o: hold both locks as long as possible
always acquire locks in the same global order (and keep critical sections short)
items.w: Deadlock needs a cycle of waiting; a global lock order removes the cycle. Timeouts on `acquire` help detect trouble.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import queue
q = queue.Queue()
q.put(1)
q.put(2)
print(q.get(), q.qsize())
```
items.w: A `Queue` is first-in first-out: `get()` returns 1, leaving one item.

items.q: *(Concept)* What does `await` do in a coroutine?
o: Suspends the coroutine until the awaited object completes, letting the event loop run other tasks meanwhile
Converts the coroutine to a generator
items.w: `await` is a cooperative yield point. The loop resumes the coroutine when the awaited result is ready.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print? (A warning about a coroutine that was never awaited may appear on standard error.)
```python
async def f():
    return 1
print(type(f()).__name__)
```
items.w: Calling an `async def` function does not run it: it returns a coroutine object that must be awaited or scheduled.

items.q: *(Concept)* A `time.sleep(2)` inside an `async def` request handler
o: blocks the whole event loop, so every other request on that worker stalls for two seconds
items.w: Cooperative scheduling: only `await` gives control back. Use `await asyncio.sleep`, or `asyncio.to_thread` for unavoidable blocking calls.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    r = await asyncio.gather(asyncio.sleep(0.02, "a"), asyncio.sleep(0.005, "b"))
    print(r)
asyncio.run(main())
```
items.w: `gather` returns results in the order of the arguments, not in completion order, and as a list.

items.q: *(Concept)* When one task in an `asyncio.TaskGroup` raises an exception, the group
o: cancels the remaining tasks and raises an `ExceptionGroup` when the block ends
returns the exception in a list
ignores it and waits for the rest
items.w: `TaskGroup` implements structured concurrency: failures cancel siblings and no task outlives the `async with` block.

items.q: *(Concept)* Inside a task, when you catch `asyncio.CancelledError` you should normally
o: do any cleanup and re-raise it
items.w: Cancellation is how timeouts and shutdown stop work. Swallowing it makes the task uncancellable.

items.q: *(Concept)* Most objects in CPython are freed
o: immediately when their reference count drops to zero
at the next full garbage collection
items.w: Reference counting is the primary mechanism; the cyclic collector only handles reference cycles.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import sys
x = []
y = x
print(sys.getrefcount(x) - 1)
```
items.w: Two names refer to the list; `getrefcount` itself adds one temporary reference, which the `- 1` removes.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which standard-library module records where memory was allocated, so you can compare snapshots to find a leak?
items.w: `tracemalloc` takes snapshots with allocation tracebacks; `compare_to` shows which lines grew.

items.q: *(Concept)* Objects that reference each other in a cycle are reclaimed by
items.w: Counts never reach zero inside a cycle, so `gc` finds unreachable cycles and frees them.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import sys
print(sys.getsizeof([1] * 3) == sys.getsizeof(["x" * 50] * 3))
```
items.w: A list stores pointers; `getsizeof` is shallow, so the size does not depend on what the items are.

items.q: *(Concept)* Python bytecode (as shown by `dis`) is
o: an implementation detail that changes between versions
items.w: Instruction sets change between releases (and 3.11+ specialises hot instructions), so never depend on bytecode and never share `.pyc` files across versions.

items.q: *(Concept)* A descriptor must be defined
o: as an attribute of a class
items.w: The attribute lookup machinery finds descriptors on the type, which is how `property`, methods and ORM fields work.
`@deco` replaces `one` with `wrapper`; without `functools.wraps` the name is the wrapper's.

items.q: *(Concept)* `__init_subclass__` is called
o: when the class is garbage collected
when a subclass of the class is defined
when the module is imported for the first time
items.w: It is a simple hook for plugin registries and validation, usually preferable to a metaclass.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
class Meta(type):
    pass
class A(metaclass=Meta):
    pass
print(type(A).__name__, isinstance(A, type))
```
items.w: A class is an instance of its metaclass, and `Meta` derives from `type`, so `A` is also an instance of `type`.

items.q: *(Concept)* Which is NOT a reliable fix for a circular import between two modules?
o: Import inside the function that needs it
Import the module and access the attribute later
Put `from a import *` at the top of both modules
Move the shared code into a third module
items.w: Star imports do not solve the ordering problem and also hide where names come from. Restructure, import the module, or defer the import.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import json
import sys
print("json" in sys.modules, json is __import__("json"))
```
items.w: A module is cached in `sys.modules`, so importing it again returns the same object.

items.q: *(Concept)* Python type hints are
o: required for the program to start
stored as metadata; checked only by external tools (mypy, pyright) or by libraries that read them, such as Pydantic
enforced by the interpreter and raise `TypeError` on mismatch
items.w: The interpreter ignores annotations at run time (it keeps them in `__annotations__`).

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
def f(x: int) -> int:
    return x
print(f("ab"))
```
items.w: The hint is not enforced, so the string passes straight through. A type checker would flag the call before running.

items.q: *(Concept)* `int | None` means the same as
items.w: `X | None` (3.10+) is the modern spelling of `Optional[X]`: the value is an int or `None`.

items.q: *(Concept)* In pytest, a fixture is
o: a way to run tests in parallel
reusable set-up (and tear-down) that tests request by naming it as a parameter
a decorator that skips a test
items.w: Fixtures are dependency injection for tests: pytest builds the named resource, passes it in, and cleans up after a `yield`.

items.q: *(Concept)* An application should lock exact dependency versions, whereas a library should
o: declare the widest compatible version ranges
pin every dependency to one exact version
items.w: A library is installed next to other packages, so narrow pins cause conflicts; the application's lock file chooses the concrete versions.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import tomllib
print(tomllib.loads('a = 1\nb = "x"'))
```
items.w: `tomllib` (3.11+) parses TOML into ordinary dicts and values; Python prints dicts with single quotes.

items.q: *(Concept)* The correct defence against SQL injection is
o: parameterised queries (placeholders), so data never becomes SQL text
items.w: Placeholders send the statement and the data separately, which removes the injection path altogether.

items.q: *(Concept)* To store user passwords you should
o: encrypt them with a key stored next to the database
hash them with a slow salted algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt through a maintained library
store them in plain text in a protected table
items.w: Password hashes must be expensive to brute-force and salted per user. Fast hashes are made for speed, which is the wrong property here.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
import secrets
print(len(secrets.token_hex(8)))
```
items.w: `token_hex(8)` returns 8 random bytes as hexadecimal text: two characters per byte.

items.q: *(Concept)* In Python, the Strategy pattern is usually implemented by
o: an abstract base class per strategy with a factory
passing a function (or other callable) as the varying behaviour
items.w: Functions are first-class, so `sorted(key=...)` is already Strategy. Classes are needed only when a strategy carries state or several methods.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from functools import cache
calls = []
@cache
def sq(n):
    calls.append(n)
    return n * n
sq(3)
sq(3)
sq(4)
print(calls)
```
items.w: The second `sq(3)` is answered from the cache, so the body runs only for 3 and 4.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why is `eval(user_input)` dangerous?
o: It executes arbitrary Python code chosen by the user
items.w: `eval` runs any expression, including `__import__("os").system(...)`. Use `ast.literal_eval`, `json.loads` or a real parser.

items.q: *(Concept)* Why do money amounts in the bank project use integer paise?
o: Binary floats cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, so totals drift; integers are exact
items.w: Exactness matters in a ledger. `Decimal` (from strings) is the other correct choice.

items.q: *(Concept)* The log analyzer reads the file through a generator because
o: files can only be read lazily
generators are faster than lists in every case
the memory use stays constant however large the file is, and processing starts immediately
it lets the file be modified while reading
items.w: Streaming keeps memory at O(1) per line, which is how multi-gigabyte logs are handled.

items.q: *(Concept)* A message consumer receives the same order twice (at-least-once delivery). The handler should be
o: idempotent, recording processed ids so a duplicate is ignored
items.w: Duplicates are a normal consequence of retries and redelivery; exactly-once effects are built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers.

items.q:
*(Code)* What does this program print?
```python
from collections import OrderedDict
c = OrderedDict(a=1, b=2, c=3)
c.move_to_end("a")
c.popitem(last=False)
print(list(c))
```
items.w: After `move_to_end("a")` the order is b, c, a; `popitem(last=False)` removes the oldest (b), leaving c, a. This is the heart of an LRU cache.

items.q: *(Concept)* Injecting a clock into the key-value store makes the code easier to test because
o: it removes the need for locks
tests can set the time instead of sleeping, so expiry is instant and deterministic
items.w: Non-deterministic dependencies (time, randomness, network) are passed in so tests control them.

items.q: *(Concept)* A token-bucket rate limiter differs from a fixed-window counter in that it
o: allows controlled bursts up to its capacity and refills smoothly, avoiding double bursts at window edges
items.w: Tokens accumulate at a fixed rate up to a cap, so short bursts are allowed and the long-run rate is bounded.

items.question: Name the three blocks of the daily loop and say which one is skipped most often.
items.answer: Read, run-and-break, retrieve. Retrieval (answering without the page) is skipped most often and gives the most learning per minute, because recalling an answer strengthens memory far more than re-reading it.

items.question: Why keep an error log?
items.answer: Each entry is a personalised list of the ideas you actually misunderstand. Reviewing it weekly directs your time to your weak spots instead of re-reading what you already know.

blocks.text: #### Final Mock Interview and What to Do Next

items.question: How should you use the cheat sheets?
items.answer: As compression of what you already learned: scan them the night before an interview and while coding. They are poor for learning a topic the first time; if a row does not trigger a clear picture, go back to the Part named next to it.

items.question: What do you do after finishing Core Python?
items.answer: Keep a daily DSA habit (the next stage), build and deploy a FastAPI service with a database (the web stage), and keep reading real code and the standard library. Breadth of practice, not another re-read, produces fluency.
